newsitem.title: UK: Ivorian cocoa mid-crop arrivals seen up - ED & F Man.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa mid-crop arrivals seen up - ED & F Man.

text.p: Arrivals of Ivorian mid-crop cocoa are estimated to have been in the region of 140,000 tonnes by end the of August, up from 61,000 at the same stage last season, UK commodity house ED & F Man said in a report.
"We believe that there was a sizeable carryover of mid-crop cocoa into the 1995/96 main crop," it said in its September cocoa crop update.
It said crop year arrivals to the end of September from the world's top cocoa producer were expected to reach 1.20 million tonnes.
"Given last season's mid-crop carryover, this is consistent with a total crop of 1.125 million tonnes in 1995/96 (Oct/Sept)," it said.
Weather conditions from March to June were favourable for new crop development, but the setting of the new crop was poor.
Relatively high rainfall during July and August has led to excellent survival of existing pods, but at the end of August the pod load was still lower than last season's exceptionally high level.
Man said Ivory Coast's Caisse de Stabilisation had been a regular seller of new crop throughout the summer months.
By the end of August, new crop sales were estimated to have reached 590,000 tonnes, 65,000 tonnes ahead of the same stage last season.
Man said reports from Ghana indicated that the 1995/96 mid-crop might have reached 40,000 tonnes. This would give total crop year production of around 390,000 tonnes.
It said setting for the 1996/97 main crop had been poor.
The damp, cool weather following the high rainfall in July and August had led to higher levels of black pod infection than have been present in recent years.
Indonesia's crop could rise to 290,000 tonnes in 1995/96, a 24 percent jump over last season's weather-affected output.
It expects Indonesian production, which has been rising by about 30,000 tonnes a year for the last four years, to maintain similar growth rate barring significant weather factors.
Malaysian output, continuing a downward trend, may only reach 105,000 tonnes in 1995/96 against 120,000 a year ago.

Falling net cocoa bean exports from October to April this season confirmed that most of the decline in production in 1994/95 was due to a fall in the cocoa area and lower yields due to low prices rather than the effects of adverse weather.
Prospects for Brazil's coming main crop were poor, Man said.
The 1995/96 main crop totalled 1.65 million bags, the lowest since 1976/77.
All indications are that the 1996/97 main crop will be considerably lower, partly due to a prolonged period of below average rainfall that has lasted since May, Man said.
